bib.title: Processing and Understanding Text (Chapter 3, Text Analytics with Python)
bib.venue: Apress, Text Analytics with Python, 1st ed.

question: How do you clean, tokenise and normalise raw text, then analyse its syntax with POS tagging, shallow, dependency and constituency parsing, in Python?
contributions: Python 2 / NLTK 3.1-3.2.1 code for sentence and word tokenisation, cleaning, contraction expansion, stopword removal, repeated-character and spelling correction, stemming and lemmatisation
Home-built POS taggers, shallow parsers, a dependency parser and a PCFG constituency parser, with test-set scores for tagging and chunking

results.claim: Hand-written regex chunk grammar scores 54.5% IOB accuracy on treebank_chunk test
results.setup: treebank_chunk chunked_sents, first 4000 train, rest test; RegexpParser with NP/ADJP/ADVP/PP/VP grammar (precision 25.0%, recall 52.5%, F 33.9%)

results.setup: treebank_chunk, 4000 train, remainder test; precision 98.4%, recall 100.0%, F 99.2%; the author calls it excellent and does not flag that the same split is small

results.claim: The same chunker on the larger conll2000 corpus drops to 66.8% IOB accuracy
results.setup: conll2000 chunked_sents: first 7,500 sentences train, remaining 3,448 test; precision 77.7%, recall 45.4%, F 57.3%
results.note: The text attributes the drop to the corpus being 'much larger'; it is more plausibly a harder, more varied test set, which the book does not test.

limits: Code is Python 2 (print statements, spacy.en, Stanford Parser 2015-04-20 jars, Windows paths); it will not run unmodified today.
Only the POS tagging and chunking experiments report scores, all on NLTK's small treebank sample (3,500 train sentences) with one run and no variance.
No evaluation of whether any normalisation step helps a downstream task; advice on which steps to use is by assertion.
Contraction map keeps one expansion per contraction (you'll -> you will, not you shall).

Dependency and constituency parsers are shown on a single sentence, with no scores. The Viterbi PCFG parser failed on out-of-vocabulary words until the sample sentence's words were added to the grammar by hand.
The author's spelling corrector is case sensitive until wrapped, and cannot fix words absent from big.txt.
practices: Tokenise sentences first, then words; use nltk.sent_tokenize and nltk.word_tokenize as the defaults (pp.108-113).
Decide whether to strip special characters before or after tokenisation by task; keep apostrophes if you plan to expand contractions (p.117-118).
Expand contractions with a CONTRACTION_MAP regex substitution that preserves the first-letter case (p.118-119).
Do not remove negations such as not and no as stopwords in sentiment analysis (pp.120-121).
Correct repeated characters one at a time and stop when WordNet recognises the word (p.122-123).
Use Norvig's edit-distance corrector against a large word-count file; more data helps coverage (p.123-128).
Choose a stemmer by trial and error; Porter is most common, Lancaster more aggressive, Snowball covers other languages (p.130-131).
Pass the right POS to the WordNet lemmatiser or it will not lemmatise (p.131-132).
Build POS taggers as a backoff chain (unigram, bigram, trigram, regex) rather than n-gram taggers alone; a classifier-based tagger does best (pp.139-142).
Avoid NLTK 3.2.0 because pos_tag() has issues (p.133).

terms.definition: a process that consists of a series of steps that should be followed to wrangle, clean, and standardize textual data into a form that could be consumed by other NLP and analytics systems
the root word, which will always be present in the dictionary, unlike a root stem
words that have little or no significance, usually the most frequent tokens in a corpus
chunks are sequences of tokens included in a group; chinks are tokens or sequences excluded from chunks
B- begins a chunk, I- is inside a chunk, O is outside any chunk
also called light parsing or chunking: group tokens into higher-level phrases without analysing internal syntax
a context-free grammar that associates a probability with each production rule; a tree's probability is the product of its productions
